title: Replay the match, but stay close
allegory: PPO is a player studying a recording of their own last match several times over, with one rule: once they would play a move more than 20% more or less often than they did on the tape, the tape stops teaching them anything about that move, so it is time to record a fresh match.
map: a recorded match of how you played
a batch of rollouts from π_old, with its logprobs stored
several epochs of minibatch gradient steps on that one batch
how much more often you would now play a move
the coach's note: better or worse than expected
the advantage A_t, from the critic via GAE
past a 20% change, the tape teaches nothing more about that move
clip(r_t, 1 − ε, 1 + ε) with ε = 0.2: zero gradient outside the band

chapters.name: Use once, bin it?
chapters.note: all those games ... used for one step?

props.label: study it once, throw it away?

cap.1: Playing games to learn from is slow. Using each batch of games once and throwing it away feels wasteful. Why not study it several times?
cap.2: REINFORCE uses each batch for one gradient step. PPO takes several steps on the same batch, far more data-efficient, and that is exactly why it needs a brake.
cap.3: Reused on-policy data is off-policy after the first step: sampled from π_old, optimised for π_θ. The surrogate objective corrects for that only while π_θ stays near π_old.

cap.1: A chess bot notices aggression paid off in its recorded games and drills that lesson again and again. Soon it is aggressive, yet still learning from its old timid games.
cap.2: After a few steps the policy has changed, so the batch describes a different agent. Keep optimising and you confidently improve an estimate that has stopped applying.
cap.3: The importance-weighted surrogate r_t·A_t is only a good local approximation near θ_old. Far from it, the estimate's error grows and a greedy optimiser exploits that error.

parts.note: how much more often, times how good

cap.1: r says how much more often you would now play a move than on the tape. Multiply by how good the move was. Past a 20% change, the credit stops growing.
cap.2: r_t = π_new(a|s) / π_old(a|s), computed as exp(new_logprob − old_logprob). Take the min of r·A and clip(r, 1 − ε, 1 + ε)·A, with ε = 0.2.
cap.3: Outside the band the clipped branch wins the min and is constant in θ, so its gradient is exactly zero: clipping removes gradient rather than rescaling it.

cap.1: For a good move, credit rises as you favour it more, then goes flat past 1.2. For a bad move, blame stops once you have cut it by 20%. Flat means no more pull.
cap.2: A > 0: the objective caps at (1 + ε)·A, so no gain from pushing probability higher. A < 0: it floors at (1 − ε)·A, so one update cannot crush an action to zero.
cap.3: The min keeps the pessimistic branch: the clip only removes the incentive to go further in the direction the advantage favours. Moves that worsen the objective are still penalised.

nodes.label: record a match: rollout with π_old
study it: a few epochs of minibatches

cap.1: The whole routine: record a match, get the coach's notes on each move, study the tape a few times under the 20% rule, then record a fresh match.
cap.2: Roll out the current policy (storing logprobs), compute GAE advantages from the critic, then run a few epochs of minibatch updates on the combined objective. Repeat.
cap.3: Objective = clipped surrogate − c₁·clipped value loss + c₂·entropy (ARENA: clip_coef 0.2, ent_coef 0.01), advantages normalised per minibatch, θ_old reset at each rollout.

chapters.name: Studied to death
chapters.verdict: Log the clip fraction. Past about a third, cut epochs or learning rate.

cap.1: Study one tape too many times and most moves hit the 20% wall. The player stops learning from it, drifts, and gets worse, though it all looks calm.
cap.2: Too many epochs push most ratios outside [1 − ε, 1 + ε], where the gradient is zero. The policy loss flatlines while return collapses. Log the clip fraction every phase.
cap.3: A healthy clip fraction sits around 5 to 20%; past roughly a third, cut update_epochs (4 is sane), minibatch passes or lr. A rising approx-KL within one batch is the same alarm: stop early.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Clip, not KL: know which is which

cap.1: This same careful routine is how chat models were taught to follow human preferences: PPO is the optimiser underneath RLHF.
cap.2: RLHF and GRPO keep PPO's clipped ratio and change the reward and baseline. PPO clips the ratio; TRPO constrains KL to the old policy; RLHF penalises KL to a frozen reference.
cap.3: Knowing what PPO's update pushes toward, and how far per batch, is the substrate for understanding and steering any RL-trained behaviour, including a fine-tuned language model's.

coda.title: Pick a good or bad move, then slide how much the policy has changed

params.label: advantage A (how good the move was)
ratio r = π_new / π_old for this move

readouts.label: pull on the ratio (slope)
readouts.f: (ratio*A <= clamp(ratio, 1 - eps, 1 + eps)*A + 1e-12) ? A.toFixed(2) : '0: clipped, no more pull'

caption.1: Pick a good or bad move with A, then slide the ratio. Where the orange line goes flat, this batch has nothing more to teach about that move.
caption.2: Positive A: flat past 1 + ε. Negative A: flat below 1 − ε. On the other side the slope survives, so a move pushed the wrong way is still corrected.
caption.3: dL/dr = A where the unclipped branch is active, 0 where the clipped branch wins the min. Smaller ε is a tighter per-batch trust region; ε = 0.2 is the paper's and ARENA's default.

where_else: RLHF: PPO's clipped update plus a KL penalty to a frozen reference model
GRPO: the same clipped ratio, with the group mean replacing the critic
TRPO: the same 'stay close' goal, enforced with an explicit KL constraint
Any surrogate objective that is trustworthy only near where you sampled it

hamming.what: A policy-gradient algorithm that takes several gradient steps on each batch of experience, clipping the probability ratio so the policy cannot drift far from the one that collected it.
hamming.when: Whenever you train an agent from its own experience, from CartPole in [2.3] to RLHF for language models.
hamming.why: It squeezes more learning out of each expensive batch while staying close enough that the batch still describes the policy being trained.

object.title: The clipped ramp
object.subtitle: Across: how much the policy changed a move. Back: how good the move was. Height: the credit PPO hands out.

marks.label: good move pushed far: flat shelf
bad move cut hard: flat floor

cap.1: The whole rule as a landscape. Across: how much more often you'd play a move. Back: how good it was. Height: the credit you get.
cap.2: L_CLIP(r, A) = min(r·A, clip(r, 1 − ε, 1 + ε)·A) over ratio and advantage, ε = 0.2.
cap.3: A piecewise-linear surface: sloped where the unclipped branch is active, flat where the clipped branch wins.

cap.1: Look along the good-move side: the ramp climbs, then goes flat past 1.2. Up on the shelf, pushing further earns nothing.
cap.2: For A > 0 the objective caps at (1 + ε)·A, so the gradient with respect to r is zero past 1 + ε.
cap.3: Zero gradient on the shelf is exact, not approximate: the surviving branch does not depend on θ.

cap.1: Now the bad-move side: the blame slope stops at 0.8. One batch cannot wipe a move out entirely.
cap.2: For A < 0 the objective floors at (1 − ε)·A below r = 1 − ε: no further push to shrink the probability.
cap.3: Above 1 + ε with A < 0 the slope survives: a bad move made more likely is still corrected.

cap.1: Loosen the rule and the flat shelves move outward: bigger steps per batch, less safety.
cap.2: ε = 0.4 widens the band where gradients flow, so each batch can move the policy further.
cap.3: Larger ε approaches the unclipped surrogate, and with it the risk of exploiting a stale batch.

cap.1: Tighten it and the shelves close in around 1: tiny, safe steps, and slow learning.
cap.2: ε = 0.05 keeps each update very close to the old policy; stable but sample-hungry.
cap.3: ε is a per-batch trust region in ratio space: a first-order stand-in for TRPO's KL constraint.

predict.q: A good move's ratio is already 1.3 and ε = 0.2. What does the clipped objective do with it?

options.t: Gives zero gradient: no more pull

predict.why: Past 1 + ε the clipped branch wins the min and is constant, so the gradient is exactly zero.

predict.q: Why does PPO need the clip when REINFORCE does not?

options.t: It reuses each batch for several steps

predict.why: After the first step the batch comes from an older policy; the clip stops you exploiting that stale data.

predict.q: Which method penalises KL against a frozen reference model?
predict.why: PPO clips the ratio, TRPO constrains KL to the old policy, and RLHF penalises KL to a frozen pretrained reference.

object.where: Any optimiser working from a surrogate that is only trustworthy nearby: trust regions, RLHF, GRPO.
